extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students or anyone learning introductory mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter introducing statements, open sentences, logical connectives (and, or, not, conditional, biconditional), truth tables, logical equivalence, and basic laws (e.g., DeMorgan). Teaches how to form, interpret, and manipulate propositional statements for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or a mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of true statements (e.g., "Every even number is divisible by 2") and false statements (e.g., "All right triangles are isosceles") are given. Non-statements (commands, questions, and sentences whose truth depends on unspecified variables) are contrasted with statements. Exercises ask students to decide whether given sentences are statements and, if so, whether they are true or false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentence (not a statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence containing variables whose truth depends on the values of those variables (e.g., "The integer x is even") is an open sentence and not a statement unless the variables are fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open sentences are often denoted P(x), P(x,y) to emphasize variable dependence. Examples include sentences about numbers or functions; they become statements only after variables are specified or quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of letters to denote statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters P, Q, R (and subscripts when needed) to stand for specific statements as a convenient shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shorthand avoids repeating long sentences; e.g., denote "The function f(x)=x^2 is continuous" by R. It is useful when forming compound statements and truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining statements with AND (∧)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement P ∧ Q (read 'P and Q') asserts that both P and Q are true; P ∧ Q is true iff both P and Q are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Examples and anti-examples illustrate that if either conjunct is false, the conjunction is false. Exercises practice expressing sentences as P ∧ Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining statements with OR (∨) — inclusive or
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement P ∨ Q (read 'P or Q') means one or both of P and Q is true; it is true if P is true, Q is true, or both are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that mathematical 'or' is inclusive and differs from some everyday uses (exclusive or). If 'exactly one' is intended, express it explicitly (e.g., 'P or Q, but not both' or 'Either P or Q'). Truth table provided and examples discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (~) and its meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation ~P means 'It is not true that P' (read 'not P') and reverses the truth value of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several equivalent English phrasings shown (e.g., 'It is false that P', 'P is not true'). Truth table for negation has two lines. Note: ~ is a unary operator and negation has syntactic precedence like a unary minus; parentheses are used to clarify scope (e.g., ~P ∨ Q means (~P) ∨ Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional/Implication (P => Q) truth condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional P => Q (read 'If P, then Q') is true in all cases except when P is true and Q is false; it asserts that whenever P is true, Q is also true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table explained and justified via examples (professor promise). Many English constructions mean the same as P => Q (e.g., 'Q if P', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'P only if Q' corresponds appropriately). Emphasizes that conditional can be true even when antecedent is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading various English forms as implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Several grammatical constructions express P => Q: 'If P, then Q', 'Q if P', 'Q whenever P', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'Q is a necessary condition for P', 'P only if Q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should analyze and be able to map these phrasings to the logical implication and understand the subtle wording differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse of a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse of P => Q is Q => P; in general the converse is logically different from the original implication and may be true or false independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that P => Q need not imply Q => P (e.g., 'multiple of 6 => divisible by 2' is true, converse is false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (↔) — if and only if
rubrics_metrics.description: P ↔ Q (read 'P if and only if Q') is the conjunction of P => Q and Q => P; it is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value (both true or both false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently read as 'P is a necessary and sufficient condition for Q'. Truth table provided and many English phrasings listed. Examples: 'a is even ↔ a is divisible by 2'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth tables for complex statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine truth-values of complex formulas, build truth tables enumerating all possible truth-value combinations of atomic statements and compute intermediate columns as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helper/intermediate columns (for subexpressions) are useful but optional if confident. Examples include two- and three-variable tables and combining ¬, ∧, ∨, =>, ↔. Exercises require constructing truth tables for given expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth values match line-for-line in a truth table (i.e., they have the same truth table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: P ↔ Q is equivalent to (P ∧ Q) ∨ (~P ∧ ~Q). Logical equivalence lets you rewrite statements into potentially more useful forms (e.g., proving P => Q may be easier by proving the contrapositive (~Q => ~P)).

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's Laws (instance shown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation distributes over conjunction and disjunction as in DeMorgan's Laws; example given: ~(P ∧ Q) = (~P) ∨ (~Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences are prevalent and useful for manipulating logical formulas. (The text labels these as Fact 2.1 and uses them repeatedly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between correct logic and correct information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the process of deducing information correctly, not guaranteeing that the information (premises) is true; a valid argument can have false premises but still be logically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by example where premises are false but the inferential steps are valid. Important for following consequences of incorrect assumptions and in mathematical proofs where one deduces consequences to test or explore assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parentheses and operator precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses are necessary to indicate grouping in complex formulas; negation (~) has unary precedence similar to algebraic unary minus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ~P ∨ Q means (~P) ∨ Q, not ~(P ∨ Q). Proper parenthesization avoids ambiguity when combining operators of different arities.
